quest_data.title: Determine Eligibility
quest_data.subtitle: Before filing, confirm that the core eligibility conditions for an IR-1 spouse petition are in place. Complete each section below.

quests.title: Petitioner is a U.S. Citizen
quests.subtitle: Confirm the petitioner qualifies to file an IR-1 spouse petition

screens.label: Petitioner Status
screens.question: What is the petitioner's current immigration status?
screens.helper: The IR-1 visa is only available when the petitioner is a U.S. citizen — not a green card holder.

options.label: U.S. citizen
Lawful Permanent Resident (green card holder)
options.sub: Spouse of LPR uses a different visa category (F2A), not IR-1.

options.label: Not sure
Other / none of these

screens.label: How Citizenship Was Obtained
screens.question: How did the petitioner become a U.S. citizen?
screens.helper: Each path to citizenship is valid for this petition. Pick the one that applies.

options.label: Born in the United States
Born abroad to a U.S. citizen parent (acquired or derived citizenship)
Naturalized (took the oath after immigrating)
Not sure

screens.label: Proof of Citizenship
screens.question: Does the petitioner have at least one accepted proof of U.S. citizenship?
screens.helper: USCIS accepts several document types. You do not need all of them — just one valid proof.

items: Valid or recently expired U.S. passport
U.S. birth certificate issued by a state or county
USCIS Certificate of Naturalization (Form N-550)
USCIS Certificate of Citizenship (Form N-560)
U.S. Consular Report of Birth Abroad (Form FS-240)

options.label: Yes — I have at least one of these documents
Not yet — but I can obtain one
No — and I'm not sure how to get one
Not sure

screens.label: Name Consistency
screens.question: Does the name on the citizenship document match the name the petitioner will use on this petition?
screens.helper: Name discrepancies are manageable with supporting documents. Flag this now so it isn't a surprise later.

options.label: Yes — name matches exactly
No — but I have legal proof of the name change
No — and I don't have name-change proof yet
Not sure

quests.title: A legally valid marriage exists
quests.subtitle: Confirm there is a current, legally recognized civil marriage

screens.label: Relationship Status
screens.question: Which of these best describes the couple's current legal relationship?
screens.helper: USCIS requires an existing, legally recognized civil marriage — not just an engagement or ceremony.

options.label: Legally married (civil registration is in place)
Only engaged — not yet married
Religious or cultural ceremony only — no civil registration
options.sub: Civil registration is typically required for immigration purposes.

options.label: Separated or in the process of divorce
Not sure

screens.label: Legal Recognition
screens.question: Was the marriage legally recognized under the laws of the place where it occurred?
screens.helper: USCIS evaluates marriage validity under the law of the place where it was celebrated. Most civil marriages are valid, but some may have local registration gaps.

options.label: Yes — it was a legally registered civil marriage there
No — it was not legally registered or recognized there
Not sure

screens.label: Marriage Certificate
screens.question: Is there an official marriage certificate or record issued by the appropriate civil authority?
screens.helper: USCIS expects the official civil marriage certificate from the relevant government or registry office — not wedding photos or invitations.

items: Government-issued marriage certificate from the country or state where you married
Certified copy from a civil registry office
Apostille or official authentication if issued abroad

options.label: Yes — I have the official certificate
Not yet — but I can obtain a certified copy
No — and I'm not sure how to get one
Not sure

quests.title: All prior marriages were legally terminated
quests.subtitle: Confirm neither spouse was still married to anyone else when this marriage occurred

screens.label: Prior Marriage History
screens.question: Before this marriage, did either spouse have any previous legally registered marriages?
screens.helper: Count any marriage that was legally registered — anywhere in the world. Religious-only or unregistered ceremonies generally do not count.

options.label: No — neither spouse had any prior legally registered marriages
Yes — the petitioner had a prior marriage
Yes — the beneficiary had a prior marriage
Yes — both had prior marriages
Not sure

screens.label: Termination Timing
screens.question: Did every prior marriage end before the date of the current marriage?
screens.helper: A prior marriage must have ended first — by final divorce, annulment, or the death of the prior spouse — before the new marriage is legally valid.

options.label: Yes — all prior marriages ended before the current marriage
No — at least one prior marriage was still ongoing
Not sure about the exact timing

screens.label: Proof of Termination
screens.question: Is there documentation showing how each prior marriage legally ended?
screens.helper: USCIS will want to see this proof for every prior marriage — for both spouses.

items: Final divorce decree or judgment
Court-issued annulment order
Death certificate of the former spouse

options.label: Yes — documentation exists for all prior marriages
Some, but not all — documentation is missing for at least one
No — no documentation yet
Not sure

quests.title: Marriage is bona fide
quests.subtitle: Screen for good-faith intent and evidence of a genuine relationship

screens.label: Genuine Intent
screens.question: When both spouses married, was it with the genuine intention to build a shared life together?
screens.helper: USCIS looks at whether the marriage was entered in good faith — not primarily for immigration purposes.

options.label: Yes — both intended a genuine marriage
No — immigration was the primary reason for the marriage
I'm not sure how to answer this

screens.label: Relationship Evidence
screens.question: Which of these types of relationship evidence do you currently have?
screens.helper: Select all that apply. Having multiple types of evidence across different categories strengthens the case significantly.

options.label: Shared address or co-habitation history
Joint finances, bank accounts, or shared bills
Photos, travel records, messages, or call logs
Children together, pregnancy, or family evidence
Statements from family, friends, or community who know the couple
None of the above yet

screens.label: Consistency
screens.question: Can both spouses describe the relationship consistently — timeline, how they met, living situation, and future plans?
screens.helper: USCIS interviews often test whether both spouses' stories match on basic facts. This is not about perfection, but about genuine shared knowledge.

options.label: Yes — both are comfortable and consistent on the basics
Mostly — there may be some minor gaps or differences
No — there are significant inconsistencies
Not sure

screens.label: Fraud Risk Flags
screens.question: Are there facts in this case that might raise questions about the relationship's authenticity?
screens.helper: This is just a flag — having a complicating factor doesn't mean the marriage isn't real. It means you'll want to address it proactively.

hint.intro: Common factors that may invite closer review:
items: Very short time between meeting and marriage (a few weeks)
Prior spousal petition filed by either spouse for a different person
Very limited documented contact or time spent together
Significant age difference with limited shared history
Prior finding of marriage fraud in either spouse's immigration history

options.label: No — no significant fraud-risk factors I can think of
Yes — there is at least one factor that may need explanation
Not sure

Start building your evidence package now — across multiple categories.' }; return { state: 'pass', title: 'Bona fide marriage looks solid', body: 'Good-faith intent is affirmed, relationship evidence exists across multiple categories, and no major fraud-risk flags were identified. This section looks strong.' }; })()

quests.title: Additional possible visa ineligibilities
quests.subtitle: Early screening for common immigrant visa admissibility concerns

screens.label: Prior Immigration Actions
screens.question: Has the beneficiary ever been refused a U.S. visa, denied an immigration benefit, ordered removed, deported, or accused of using fraud or misrepresentation in any immigration matter?
screens.helper: Prior refusals don't automatically disqualify a case. But fraud or misrepresentation can be a serious bar to admissibility.

options.label: No — none of the above
Yes — at least one of these applies
Not sure

screens.label: Criminal History
screens.question: Does the beneficiary have any arrest, charge, or criminal conviction — anywhere in the world?
screens.helper: Even minor or older matters can affect immigration eligibility. Do not guess or omit — certain convictions can trigger bars to admissibility.

options.label: No — no arrests, charges, or convictions
Yes — there is at least one arrest, charge, or conviction
Not sure

screens.label: Health & Medical
screens.question: Is there any known health issue that might arise during the required immigration medical exam?
screens.helper: The beneficiary must pass a medical exam by a USCIS-designated physician. This screen only asks whether there's a known concern to plan around.

hint.intro: Medical grounds of inadmissibility can include:
items: Certain communicable diseases of public health significance
Failure to have required immigration vaccinations
Certain documented substance use disorders

options.label: No known health concern for the medical exam
Yes — there is a health concern that may come up
Not sure

screens.label: Prior U.S. Immigration History
screens.question: Has the beneficiary ever entered the U.S. without inspection, overstayed a visa, or accumulated unlawful presence in the United States?
screens.helper: Unlawful presence can trigger multi-year or permanent bars to admissibility depending on the amount of time and how departure occurred.

options.label: No — the beneficiary has no such U.S. immigration history
Yes — at least one of these applies
Not sure

screens.label: Financial Sponsorship
screens.question: Is there any concern that meeting the financial sponsorship requirements (Affidavit of Support) may be difficult?
screens.helper: This does not affect eligibility right now — it's a forward-looking flag to plan for. The petitioner will need to meet the minimum income threshold or secure a joint sponsor.

options.label: No known concern — petitioner can likely meet the income requirement
Yes — there may be a challenge meeting the income threshold
Not sure yet

filing_data.title: Decide Filing Method
filing_data.subtitle: Choose how to file Form I-130 with USCIS. Both methods are fully accepted and take the same amount of time to process — select the one that works best for you.

methods.title: PAPER FILING

screens.question: Is an attorney or accredited representative managing the filing for you?
screens.helper: If a representative is handling the paperwork, they typically decide the filing method — this walkthrough may not apply.

items: Attorneys can file I-130 online via their USCIS representative account, or by mailing a paper packet — both work
Ask your attorney or document preparer which method they prefer before deciding

options.label: Yes — a representative is handling this
No — I'm filing on my own
Not sure yet

screens.question: Can the petitioner create and manage a USCIS online account?
screens.helper: Online filing requires a free USCIS account at my.uscis.gov — used to complete the form, upload documents, and pay the filing fee.

items: Account setup takes a few minutes and just needs a valid email address
Your USCIS account also delivers notices, requests for evidence, and case updates
Paper filers can add their case to a USCIS account later using the mailed receipt number

options.label: Yes — comfortable setting up and using an online account
No — online accounts aren't practical right now
Not sure

screens.question: Are the required documents available in digital form for upload?
screens.helper: Online filing requires uploading scanned or photographed copies. Paper filing uses physical copies sent by mail.

items: PDF, JPG, or PNG are accepted — a phone camera usually works fine
Documents must be clear and fully legible
A flatbed scanner gives better results for dense documents like a Nikah Nama

options.label: Yes — documents are ready or easy to scan
No — physical copies only, hard to digitize right now
Not sure

screens.question: Does the petitioner have a preference for how to file?
screens.helper: Both methods are fully valid. Your comfort level is a legitimate deciding factor — there is no wrong choice.

options.label: Prefer online — convenient and saves $50
Prefer paper — more comfortable mailing a physical packet
No strong preference — happy with whatever works best

tutorial_steps.label: Step 1 of 10 — Sign in to USCIS
tutorial_steps.heading: Sign in to your USCIS account
tutorial_steps.instruction: Go to myaccount.uscis.gov and sign in with the email address and password you set up when creating the account. Complete the two-step verification prompt.
tutorial_steps.note: Two-step verification is required on every login — have your phone or authenticator app ready.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 2 of 10 — Go to myUSCIS
tutorial_steps.heading: Navigate to myUSCIS
tutorial_steps.instruction: After signing in, you will be directed to the myUSCIS portal homepage. This is your central hub for filing forms, checking case status, and managing your USCIS cases.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 3 of 10 — MyUSCIS Account Homepage
tutorial_steps.heading: View your account homepage
tutorial_steps.instruction: Your myUSCIS account homepage displays your filed cases, notices, and filing options. This is where you will manage all your online USCIS applications.
tutorial_steps.screenDesc: Your account home and filing hub

tutorial_steps.label: Step 4 of 10 — File a Form Online
tutorial_steps.heading: Click 'File a Form Online'
tutorial_steps.instruction: From your account homepage, locate and click the "File a Form Online" button. This is the starting point for all online form submissions.
tutorial_steps.note: If you don't see this button immediately, scroll down — its position may vary on the dashboard.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 5 of 10 — Select Form I-130
tutorial_steps.heading: Find and select Form I-130
tutorial_steps.instruction: After clicking "File a Form Online," you will see a list of available forms. Locate Form I-130, Petition for Alien Relative and select it to begin.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 6 of 10 — Review Filing Methods
tutorial_steps.heading: Confirm your filing method
tutorial_steps.instruction: USCIS may ask you to confirm your filing preference: guided online workflow or PDF upload method. Choose the guided online workflow for step-by-step assistance.
tutorial_steps.screenDesc: Select guided online or PDF upload

tutorial_steps.label: Step 7 of 10 — Begin the I-130 Form
tutorial_steps.heading: Start filling out Form I-130
tutorial_steps.instruction: The USCIS portal will walk you through the form section by section. Enter your information carefully — progress saves automatically as you go.
tutorial_steps.note: You can save your progress and return later to continue — the system will remember where you left off.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 8 of 10 — Fill Required Fields
tutorial_steps.heading: Complete all required sections
tutorial_steps.instruction: Fill in all required fields carefully and accurately. Your answers must match your official documents. Check twice before moving to the next section.
tutorial_steps.note: Inconsistencies between your form and official documents can lead to a Request for Evidence (RFE) — take time to be accurate.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 9 of 10 — Go to I-130A Section
tutorial_steps.heading: Complete Form I-130A for beneficiary
tutorial_steps.instruction: After completing the I-130, you will proceed to Form I-130A — the supplemental form for information about the beneficiary (your spouse). Fill this section with your spouse's details.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 10 of 10 — Upload I-130A Form
tutorial_steps.heading: Upload the completed I-130A
tutorial_steps.instruction: After completing Form I-130A, upload it along with your supporting evidence. Ensure all files are clearly named, legible, and in PDF or JPG format.
tutorial_steps.note: All documents must be under 12 MB each. Foreign-language documents require certified English translations uploaded separately.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 1 of 4 — Locate the Evidence Section
tutorial_steps.heading: Find the evidence upload section
tutorial_steps.instruction: Inside your I-130 draft, navigate to the evidence or supporting documents section. USCIS labels this as the upload step in the guided online filing workflow.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 2 of 4 — Upload Documents
tutorial_steps.heading: Attach your supporting evidence
tutorial_steps.instruction: Upload each document individually using the upload interface. Select and attach all required documents: passport, marriage certificate, civil documents, photos, and any other evidence supporting your petition.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 3 of 4 — Review Each File

tutorial_steps.label: Step 1 of 4 — Watch for USCIS acceptance
tutorial_steps.heading: Look for the first accepted-filing notice
tutorial_steps.instruction: After USCIS accepts the filing, watch your USCIS online account, any available e-notification, and the physical notice by mail. The goal is to bring back the receipt number once it appears.
tutorial_steps.ssDesc: Any of these may be the first place you notice the case has been accepted.
tutorial_steps.caption: Return to Rahvana once you have the receipt number or the notice itself.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 2 of 4 — Find the receipt number
tutorial_steps.heading: Find the 13-character receipt number
tutorial_steps.instruction: The receipt number is the core tracking identifier. It consists of 3 letters followed by 10 numbers, such as IOE1234567890.
tutorial_steps.ssDesc: Common prefixes include IOE, EAC, WAC, LIN, SRC, NBC, or MSC.
tutorial_steps.caption: This is the number Rahvana should save to enable case monitoring.
tutorial_steps.note: If the notice contains multiple numbers, prioritize the USCIS receipt number tied to the I-130 filing.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 3 of 4 — Decide how to register it
tutorial_steps.heading: Choose the easiest intake path
tutorial_steps.instruction: If you already have the document, upload the notice. If you only have the receipt number from the portal or an e-notification, manual entry is faster.
tutorial_steps.ssHeadline: Upload Notice or Enter Receipt Number
tutorial_steps.ssDesc: Both paths end in the same confirmation and tracked-case state.
tutorial_steps.caption: Upload is useful for preserving the notice. Manual entry is useful when speed matters more.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 4 of 4 — Save and turn on monitoring
tutorial_steps.heading: Confirm the details and enable tracking
tutorial_steps.instruction: Before saving, confirm the receipt number and any dates shown on the notice. After that, Rahvana can store the case record, enable tracking, and keep a timeline of changes.
tutorial_steps.ssDesc: Status history and notifications should begin from the saved baseline.
tutorial_steps.ssHighlight: Store receipt number → Save baseline status
tutorial_steps.caption: For IR-1, saving the priority date is useful for records, but it should not dominate this step.
tutorial_steps.note: This prototype represents tracking honestly: monitored status checks and notifications, not a promise of an official USCIS developer-grade API.

tutorial_steps.instruction: After USCIS approves your I-130 petition, your case is transferred to the National Visa Center (NVC). The NVC sends a Welcome Letter or email to the petitioner's address — this communication contains the two key details you need to access CEAC.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: Check both physical mail and email. The letter may arrive weeks after I-130 approval. The subject line typically references your NVC Case Number.
tutorial_steps.note: Check both physical mail and email. The letter may arrive weeks after I-130 approval. The subject line typically references your NVC Case Number.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 2 of 5 — Locate your NVC Case Number
tutorial_steps.heading: Locate your NVC Case Number
tutorial_steps.instruction: The NVC Case Number appears clearly in the Welcome Letter or email. For IR-1 spouse cases from Pakistan, it typically follows a format like ISL2026XXXXXX — beginning with your consulate code, followed by the year and case digits.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: ISL2026XXXXXX

tutorial_steps.label: Step 3 of 5 — Locate your Invoice ID Number
tutorial_steps.heading: Locate your Invoice ID Number
tutorial_steps.instruction: The Invoice ID Number (also called the Invoice Identification Number) also appears in the same letter. This is a separate number from the case number and is required alongside it to complete first-time CEAC login.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX
tutorial_steps.note: Both the NVC Case Number and the Invoice ID are required for CEAC login. Neither alone is sufficient.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 4 of 5 — Enter your details into CEAC
tutorial_steps.heading: Enter your case details into CEAC
tutorial_steps.instruction: Go to the CEAC portal and enter your NVC Case Number and Invoice ID Number to access your case for the first time. This creates your CEAC session and allows you to begin the immigrant visa application process.

tool_data.title: Prepare Civil Documents
tool_data.subtitle: Review and prepare the civil documents needed for NVC / CEAC document upload and later consular interview readiness.

items.title: Beneficiary Passport Biographic Page
items.sub: Current passport page showing photo and personal details

items.title: Birth Certificate
items.sub: Beneficiary's civil birth record

items.title: Marriage Certificate / Marriage Registration Record
items.sub: Official civil proof of the marriage — Nikah Nama and NADRA MRC

sections.c: For Pakistan-origin cases, this typically means both the Nikah Nama (the Islamic marriage contract) and the NADRA Marriage Registration Certificate (MRC). Both together form the complete civil marriage record.
The marriage record should align with what was submitted during the I-130 USCIS stage. Ensure names, dates, and spelling are consistent.
The Nikah Nama (in Urdu) requires a full certified English translation. The NADRA MRC is bilingual but may still require a certified translation for CEAC upload.
Older Nikah Namas may have faded or handwritten entries. Ensure scans are fully legible before upload.

items.title: Police Certificate
items.sub: Pakistan Police Character Certificate (PCC) for the beneficiary

items.title: Certified English Translations
items.sub: Required for all non-English civil documents

sections.c: Every document not in English must be accompanied by a full certified English translation. This applies to all stages — USCIS, NVC, and consular.
A certification statement from the translator attesting that they are competent to translate from the source language to English and that the translation is accurate and complete.
Upload the original document and its translation as separate files or clearly labeled together. CEAC expects both — original and translation — for each non-English document.
Do not translate only part of a document. The entire document must be translated. Partial translations may trigger an RFE or document request from NVC.

items.title: Prior Marriage Termination Documents
items.sub: Required if either spouse was previously married

sections.c: If either the petitioner or beneficiary was previously married, CEAC will require proof that every prior marriage legally ended before the current marriage.

• Final divorce decree or judgment
  • Annulment order
  • Death certificate of former spouse

For talaq in Pakistan: the divorce is not legally effective until the 90-day reconciliation period expires and the Union Council issues the final divorce certificate. Ensure you have the final certificate, not just the initial notice.
All termination documents in Urdu must be accompanied by certified English translations.

items.title: Death Certificate of Former Spouse
items.sub: Only if prior marriage ended by death

sections.c: Required only if a prior marriage ended because of the death of the former spouse. A death certificate from the appropriate civil authority is needed.
If in Urdu or another language, a certified English translation is required alongside the original.

items.title: Name Change Documents
items.sub: Legal proof of any name change used in the case

sections.c: If the beneficiary's name in the passport or marriage record differs from the name used in other documents due to a legal name change, documentation of that change is required.

• Court order for name change
  • Marriage certificate showing a change of surname

items.title: Missing Document / Record Unavailability Evidence
items.sub: When a required record genuinely does not exist

sections.c: If a required document — such as a birth certificate or civil record — is genuinely unavailable or was never issued, substitute documentation may be submitted.

• A statement from the relevant civil authority confirming the record does not exist
  • Secondary evidence supporting the missing fact (hospital records, school records, etc.)
  • Personal affidavit explaining the circumstances
Missing-document submissions require careful handling. Consult an immigration attorney if a key civil record is unavailable before uploading substitutes.

items.title: Organized Translation Set
items.sub: All translations paired and labeled with their originals

sections.c: Keeping each original and its certified translation clearly paired and labeled reduces the chance of upload errors in CEAC and makes case review easier.

• Name each file pair clearly: e.g., "NikahNama_Original.pdf" and "NikahNama_Translation.pdf"
  • Group translations by person and document type before upload

items.title: Upload-Ready File Copies
items.sub: Clean, legible, properly formatted scan set

sections.c: CEAC has a 4 MB file size limit per upload. Files must be clear, legible, and properly cropped with no missing edges.

• Use consistent file naming across the packet
  • Verify each file opens correctly and is fully readable
  • PDF format is generally preferable for multi-page documents
If files are larger than 4 MB, use Rahvana's Document Vault compression tool to bring them within the CEAC upload limit.

items.title: Relationship Evidence Backup Set
items.sub: Supporting bona fide marriage evidence for later use

sections.c: While relationship evidence is not a core NVC civil document, having an organized backup set ready ensures you are prepared for any document requests or interview questions about the marriage.

• Photos together (wedding and casual, across different dates)
  • Communication history samples
  • Travel/visit documentation
  • Financial ties or joint records

guide_card.title: Step-by-Step Document Preparation Guide
guide_card.subtitle: Walk through scanning, organizing, translating, and preparing civil documents for CEAC upload.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 1 of 13 — Sign in to CEAC
tutorial_steps.heading: Sign in to CEAC
tutorial_steps.instruction: Enter CEAC using your NVC Case Number and Invoice ID from the Welcome Letter. Your fees must be fully processed and DS-260 completed before you can upload civil documents.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: Sign in with Case Number and Invoice ID
tutorial_steps.caption: Login credentials are found in your NVC Welcome Letter.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 2 of 13 — Submit IV and AOS fees
tutorial_steps.heading: Confirm all fees are paid
tutorial_steps.instruction: Before document submission begins, verify in CEAC that both the Affidavit of Support fee ($120) and the Immigrant Visa fee ($345) have been successfully processed.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: AOS + IV fees required before document upload
tutorial_steps.caption: If fees are not marked as paid, do not proceed — contact NVC first.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 3 of 13 — Start civil document upload
tutorial_steps.heading: Navigate to the civil documents section
tutorial_steps.screenTitle: Navigate to the civil documents section
tutorial_steps.instruction: In CEAC, locate and open the civil documents upload area. This is where you will attach the required birth certificates, marriage records, police certificates, and other supporting documents.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: Begin document submission
tutorial_steps.caption: Ensure all documents are scanned, organized, and renamed before beginning uploads.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 4 of 13 — Upload documents to CEAC
tutorial_steps.heading: Upload each document individually
tutorial_steps.instruction: Select and upload each civil document one by one. Ensure each file is under 4 MB. For non-English documents, upload both the original and the certified English translation as separate files.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: PDF or image files, max 4 MB each
tutorial_steps.caption: CEAC uploads are processed individually — you will see feedback for each file.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 5 of 13 — Upload documents one by one
tutorial_steps.heading: Process each upload sequentially
tutorial_steps.instruction: Continue uploading remaining documents one at a time. CEAC will show the upload progress for each file. Wait for confirmation before uploading the next document.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: One document at a time — wait for confirmation
tutorial_steps.caption: Uploading sequentially helps you track which documents have been processed.
tutorial_steps.note: Do not close the browser tab during the upload process.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 6 of 13 — Upload all required documents
tutorial_steps.heading: Complete the full civil document set
tutorial_steps.screenTitle: Complete the full civil document set
tutorial_steps.instruction: Upload all required civil documents as per CEAC's document type list. Include birth certificates, marriage records, police certificates, and all certified English translations. Verify each upload is confirmed before moving to the next.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: Required documents checklist completed
tutorial_steps.caption: Use Rahvana's civil document checklist as your reference during uploads.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 7 of 13 — Document unavailable? Use comments
tutorial_steps.heading: Report missing or unavailable documents
tutorial_steps.instruction: If a required document is genuinely unavailable or does not exist, use the comments field to explain why. Provide a brief, clear explanation of the circumstance and any substitute documents you have submitted instead.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: Use comments to document unavailability
tutorial_steps.caption: Be concise and factual — explain only what is genuinely unavailable, not what is incomplete.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 8 of 13 — Write comments for missing documents
tutorial_steps.heading: Document your explanation in comments
tutorial_steps.instruction: In the comment section, write a clear explanation for any document that is unavailable. Include the document name, reason for unavailability, and any substitute documents submitted. Keep the explanation brief and professional.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: Provide context for missing documents
tutorial_steps.caption: Example: 'Birth certificate was lost in a flood in 2015. Submitted secondary evidence including school and medical records instead.'

tutorial_steps.label: Step 9 of 13 — Document rejected? Review and correct
tutorial_steps.heading: Review rejection reasons and correct issues
tutorial_steps.screenTitle: Review rejection reasons and correct issues
tutorial_steps.instruction: If a document is rejected by CEAC, you will see an explanation of why — it may be file size, format, legibility, or missing information. Review the reason carefully and prepare a corrected version of the document.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: Review rejection reason and resubmit corrected file
tutorial_steps.caption: Common rejection reasons: file too large (over 4 MB), image too blurry, or missing required pages.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 10 of 13 — Re-upload rejected documents
tutorial_steps.heading: Upload the corrected document
tutorial_steps.instruction: After correcting the issue, re-upload the document following CEAC's process. If the file was too large, try compressing it. If it was blurry, rescan it at higher resolution (300 DPI minimum). Upload the corrected version and wait for confirmation.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: Resubmit corrected document
tutorial_steps.caption: Use Rahvana's Document Vault compression tool if file size is the issue.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 11 of 13 — Document accepted
tutorial_steps.heading: Confirmation that document was accepted
tutorial_steps.instruction: Once a document is accepted by CEAC, you will see an approval message or status change. The document is now part of your official case record. Continue uploading remaining documents until all required documents are submitted.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: File is now in case record
tutorial_steps.caption: Each accepted document moves you one step closer to documentary qualification.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 12 of 13 — Check submission status
tutorial_steps.heading: Verify your overall submission status
tutorial_steps.instruction: After uploading all civil documents, check the overall status in CEAC to confirm all items have been received and are marked as 'Submitted' or 'Received.' This gives you confidence before proceeding.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: Confirm all documents marked as received
tutorial_steps.caption: Document submission is a milestone — once completed, NVC will begin reviewing your package for documentary qualification.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 13 of 13 — Case ready for NVC review
tutorial_steps.heading: Your case is ready for NVC processing
tutorial_steps.screenTitle: Your case is ready for NVC processing
tutorial_steps.instruction: With all required civil documents submitted and accepted, your case package is now ready for NVC's documentary qualification review. NVC will now examine your complete case to determine whether all required documents are present and consistent before issuing a DQ (Documentary Qualification) notice.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: Awaiting Documentary Qualification determination
tutorial_steps.caption: NVC document review typically takes 4-8 weeks. Monitor your email and CEAC case status for updates.

guide_card.title: Step-by-Step Affidavit of Support Guide
guide_card.subtitle: Walk through paying sponsorship fees, submitting financial documents, and uploading supporting evidence to CEAC.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 1 of 8 — Pay Affidavit of Support fee
tutorial_steps.heading: Pay the AOS sponsorship fee
tutorial_steps.instruction: In CEAC, navigate to the fee section and pay the Affidavit of Support fee ($120 as of 2026). This fee is required before financial documentation can be submitted. Use your CEAC account to complete the payment.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: $120 required payment
tutorial_steps.caption: AOS fee is separate from the Immigrant Visa fee — both must be paid before document submission.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 2 of 8 — Receive AOS payment receipt
tutorial_steps.heading: Confirm payment and save receipt
tutorial_steps.instruction: After successfully paying the AOS fee, CEAC will display a payment receipt or confirmation. Save or print this confirmation for your records as proof that the fee has been paid.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: Save receipt for your records
tutorial_steps.caption: The receipt confirms the fee payment and allows you to proceed with submitting sponsorship documents.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 3 of 8 — Start AOS and financial document submission
tutorial_steps.heading: Begin the Affidavit of Support document submission
tutorial_steps.screenTitle: Begin the Affidavit of Support document submission
tutorial_steps.instruction: Once the AOS fee is paid, navigate to the Affidavit of Support section in CEAC. This is where you will upload the completed I-864 or I-864EZ form and all supporting financial documents for the petitioner and any joint sponsors or household members.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: Prepare to upload AOS forms and financial evidence
tutorial_steps.caption: Have all financial documents ready: tax returns, W-2s, pay stubs, bank statements, and employment letters.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 4 of 8 — Select and verify document type
tutorial_steps.heading: Check the document type before uploading
tutorial_steps.screenTitle: Check the document type before uploading
tutorial_steps.instruction: CEAC requires you to specify the document type for each file (e.g., Tax Return, W-2, Affidavit of Support form, etc.). Verify that you are selecting the correct document type from CEAC's dropdown menu before uploading each file.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: Verify correct type before upload
tutorial_steps.caption: Incorrectly classified documents may be rejected or cause confusion during NVC review — always verify the type first.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 5 of 8 — Upload financial documents
tutorial_steps.heading: Upload each financial document
tutorial_steps.instruction: Upload all required financial documents one by one. Ensure each file is under 4 MB, clearly labeled, and in PDF or image format. Include tax returns, W-2 forms, pay stubs, bank statements, employment letters, and any other evidence of income or assets required to support the I-864 sponsorship.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: Tax returns, W-2s, pay stubs, bank statements
tutorial_steps.caption: Upload files in the order they are requested by CEAC to keep the submission organized.
tutorial_steps.note: Do not close the browser tab during the upload process.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 6 of 8 — Verify submission completeness
tutorial_steps.heading: Check that all documents are submitted
tutorial_steps.screenTitle: Check that all documents are submitted
tutorial_steps.instruction: After uploading all financial documents, review the submission checklist in CEAC to confirm that all required documents have been received and are marked as 'Submitted' or 'Accepted.' This ensures your AOS package is complete.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: All required AOS documents submitted
tutorial_steps.caption: A complete AOS submission is necessary for NVC to determine documentary qualification.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 7 of 8 — Document rejected? Review reason
tutorial_steps.heading: Understand why a document was rejected
tutorial_steps.screenTitle: Understand why a document was rejected
tutorial_steps.instruction: If a financial document is rejected by CEAC, you will see a rejection reason. Common reasons include: file too large (over 4 MB), image too blurry, missing pages, or incorrect document type. Review the reason carefully and prepare a corrected version.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: Review reason and prepare corrected file
tutorial_steps.caption: Re-scan blurry documents at 300 DPI and compress large files using Rahvana's Document Vault tool.

tutorial_steps.label: Step 8 of 8 — Replace rejected document
tutorial_steps.heading: Re-upload the corrected document
tutorial_steps.instruction: After correcting the issue, re-upload the document using CEAC's resubmission process. Ensure the new file meets all requirements: under 4 MB, clear and legible, correct document type selected. Upload and wait for confirmation that the document is now accepted.
tutorial_steps.ss_desc: Resubmit corrected financial document
tutorial_steps.caption: Once accepted, your AOS package will be considered complete and ready for NVC documentary qualification review.

household_member.label: Step 1 of 7 — Add household member
household_member.heading: Add a household member to your sponsorship

household_member.instruction: In CEAC, navigate to the sponsorship section and select the option to add a household member. A household member is someone who lives with the petitioner and whose income contributes to meeting the affidavit of support income requirement.
household_member.ss_desc: Add a person living in the petitioner's household
household_member.caption: Household members can include adult children, parents, siblings, or others living in the same residence.

household_member.label: Step 2 of 7 — Add household member documents
household_member.heading: Upload household member's financial documents
household_member.instruction: Select and upload the required financial documents for the household member. These typically include tax returns, W-2 forms, pay stubs, and bank statements showing their income and assets.
household_member.ss_desc: Tax returns, W-2s, pay stubs, bank statements
household_member.caption: Ensure documents are under 4 MB and clearly labeled before upload.

household_member.label: Step 3 of 7 — Receive confirmation message
household_member.heading: Confirmation that household member was added
household_member.screenTitle: Confirmation that household member was added
household_member.instruction: CEAC will display a confirmation message once the household member and their documents have been successfully received. Save this confirmation for your records.
household_member.caption: The household member is now part of your sponsorship package.

household_member.label: Step 4 of 7 — Approval of household member addition
household_member.heading: Household member addition approved
household_member.instruction: Once CEAC has reviewed and approved the household member addition, you will see an approval status. This confirms that their income is now counted toward your affidavit of support income requirement.
household_member.ss_desc: Income now counted in sponsorship package
household_member.caption: Approval typically takes several business days after submission.

household_member.label: Step 6 of 7 — Upload financial documents

household_member.instruction: Upload the complete financial document set for both the petitioner and the household member. Ensure each file is under 4 MB and in the correct format (PDF or image). Submit documents one by one and wait for confirmation.
household_member.ss_desc: Complete financial package for both sponsors

joint_sponsor.instruction: In CEAC, navigate to the sponsorship section and select the option to add a joint sponsor. A joint sponsor is a separate person (typically with significant income and assets) who jointly files the Affidavit of Support with the petitioner.

joint_sponsor.instruction: Select and upload the required financial documents for the joint sponsor. Include their complete tax returns (3 years), W-2 forms, current pay stubs (6 months), bank statements, and employment verification letter.

joint_sponsor.screenTitle: Confirmation that joint sponsor was added

joint_sponsor.label: Step 4 of 8 — Approval of joint sponsor addition

joint_sponsor.instruction: Once CEAC has reviewed and approved the joint sponsor addition, you will see an approval status. This confirms that the joint sponsor is now officially part of your affidavit of support package and their income is counted.
joint_sponsor.ss_desc: Income now counted in I-864 package
joint_sponsor.caption: Approval confirms both the petitioner and joint sponsor can meet the income requirement.

joint_sponsor.label: Step 5 of 8 — Start financial document submission
joint_sponsor.heading: Begin Affidavit of Support submission
joint_sponsor.instruction: After the joint sponsor is approved, navigate to the Affidavit of Support section in CEAC. You will now submit the completed I-864 form and all supporting financial documents for both the petitioner and joint sponsor.
joint_sponsor.ss_desc: Begin uploading I-864 and financial evidence
joint_sponsor.caption: Ensure the I-864 form is completed and signed before uploading.

joint_sponsor.label: Step 6 of 8 — Confirm submission status
joint_sponsor.heading: Verify submission is complete
joint_sponsor.instruction: After uploading all required Affidavit of Support documents (I-864 form, tax returns, pay stubs, bank statements for both petitioner and joint sponsor), check the submission status in CEAC to confirm all items have been received.
joint_sponsor.caption: A complete submission is critical for NVC documentary qualification.

joint_sponsor.label: Step 7 of 8 — Check document status
joint_sponsor.heading: Check the status of your submission
joint_sponsor.screenTitle: Check the status of your submission
joint_sponsor.instruction: Review the overall status of your Affidavit of Support submission in CEAC. All documents for both the petitioner and joint sponsor should show as received or accepted. This indicates your complete financial package is ready for NVC review.
joint_sponsor.ss_desc: All AOS documents confirmed in system
joint_sponsor.caption: Monitor CEAC regularly for any update notices or document requests.

joint_sponsor.label: Step 8 of 8 — Add additional documents if needed
joint_sponsor.heading: Submit any additional supporting documents
joint_sponsor.instruction: If needed, you can add additional financial documents or supporting evidence through CEAC. This may include updated pay stubs, recent bank statements, or any other documents that strengthen your sponsorship case.
joint_sponsor.caption: Additional documents can be submitted at any time during CEAC processing.

steps.step_description: Assemble the original hard-copy documents needed for your consular interview. Review each item and organize your packet carefully before interview day.

items.title: Passport (current + any prior passports)
items.sub: Bring originals of all passports — current and expired — that contain U.S. visa history

sections.c: Bring the original current passport with at least 6 months validity beyond the interview date. Also bring any prior passports that may contain relevant U.S. visa history.
Bring one photocopy of the biographic page of each passport in a separate section from the originals.

items.title: Original Birth Certificate
items.sub: Beneficiary's official civil birth record

sections.c: The original NADRA-issued CBRC or other official birth certificate. If you have an older Union Council record, bring both the original and the NADRA CBRC if available.
Bring the original Urdu certificate and the certified English translation together in the same tab.

items.title: Original Marriage Certificate / Nikah Nama
items.sub: Original Nikah Nama and NADRA MRC, plus translations

sections.c: Bring the original Nikah Nama and the NADRA Marriage Registration Certificate. Both should be accompanied by their certified English translations.
Do not submit photocopies at the window unless asked. Bring originals first and let the consular officer direct you.

items.title: Original Police Clearance Certificate (Fresh)
items.sub: The fresh PCC obtained for this interview cycle

sections.c: Bring the original fresh PCC obtained during Chapter 3 Step 3. Do not bring the older PCC submitted during NVC processing — this must be the fresh one.
Confirm the PCC is still within the validity window for your embassy. Some posts specify a maximum age for the PCC at interview.

items.title: Interview Appointment Letter
items.sub: The original printed NVC interview appointment letter

sections.c: Print and bring the original interview appointment letter received from NVC. This is your primary identification for entry into the embassy grounds.

items.title: Original Affidavit of Support — Petitioner
items.sub: Original signed I-864 or I-864EZ from the petitioner

sections.c: Bring the original signed Affidavit of Support. This must be the wet-ink signed original, not a photocopy.

items.title: DS-260 Confirmation Page
items.sub: Online Immigrant Visa Application Confirmation

sections.c: Bring the printed DS-260 confirmation page with barcode. This confirms you have successfully submitted your online immigrant visa application.
Make sure all information in your DS-260 form is accurate and matches your supporting documents such as passport and civil records.
You can download and print the confirmation page after submitting your DS-260 form from the Consular Electronic Application Center (CEAC) website.

items.title: Most Recent Tax Evidence — Petitioner
items.sub: Federal tax return or IRS transcript copies

sections.c: Bring copies of the most recent year's tax return or IRS transcript. Originals are not always required — copies are generally acceptable, but bring them organized.

items.title: Employment Letter — Petitioner
items.sub: Current employment confirmation letter if available

sections.c: If the petitioner's current employer can provide an employment letter, bring it as supporting evidence of current income. Not always required but useful to have.

items.title: Passport-Style Photos
items.sub: 2–4 recent passport-style photos meeting embassy specifications

sections.c: Bring 2–4 recent passport-style photos. Check your specific embassy's photo requirements for size and background specifications. US Embassy Pakistan typically requires standard 2x2 inch photos.

items.title: Polio Vaccination Certificate (Original)
items.sub: The original polio vaccination certificate from an approved site

sections.c: Bring the original polio vaccination certificate obtained in Step 2. The panel physician should have already reviewed it, but bring the original in case it is requested at the window.

items.title: Medical Examination Results Packet Reference
items.sub: Not brought by you — sealed by physician — but confirm it was sent

sections.c: The medical examination results are sealed by the panel physician and sent directly to the embassy. You do not carry the medical packet yourself. Confirm with your physician that the results were submitted before your interview date.

items.title: Courier Registration Certificate
items.sub: Proof of courier service registration for passport delivery

sections.c: Bring a printed copy of your courier registration confirmation. This shows where your passport and visa will be delivered after approval.
Ensure the selected courier location and contact details are correct. Any mistake may delay the delivery of your passport.
You can register and download your courier confirmation from the official portal: Register Courier Service.

items.title: Labeled Folder System or Document Binder
items.sub: Organized tabs separating each document group

sections.c: A well-organized packet makes it easier to quickly produce any document the officer requests. Disorganized packets slow down the interview and create unnecessary stress.

• Use a clear-pocket binder or labeled folder tabs
  • Label each section clearly: Passport / Civil / Financial / Extras
  • Keep originals in one section, copies in another

items.title: Full Photocopy Set of All Documents
items.sub: One complete photocopy set kept separate from originals

sections.c: Consular officers may retain copies of certain documents. Having a pre-prepared copy set means you don't risk giving away originals unnecessarily.

tutorial.label: Step 1 of 8
tutorial.heading: Prepare the night before
tutorial.instruction: The night before your interview, lay out your complete document packet, confirm your appointment letter is printed, and ensure your transport to the embassy is planned. Do not leave anything to the morning.
tutorial.visual:
Night-before checklist
Appointment letter printed Ready
Document packet organized Ready
Transport arranged Confirmed
Passport photos packed Ready
Originals and copies separated Done

tutorial.label: Step 2 of 8
tutorial.heading: Arrive early — embassy entry is strict
tutorial.instruction: Arrive at the embassy at least 20–30 minutes before your scheduled appointment time. Embassy security queues can be slow. Latecomers may not be admitted for their scheduled slot.
tutorial.note: Do not carry electronics beyond what is permitted by the embassy. Check the specific embassy's guidelines on phones and devices before arrival.
tutorial.visual:
Arrival guidance
Plan for 20–30 minutes of buffer time. Factor in traffic, parking, and security queue length — especially at high-volume posts like Islamabad or Karachi.
Earlier is always safer than exactly on time

tutorial.label: Step 3 of 8
tutorial.heading: Security screening and document intake
tutorial.instruction: At entry, your appointment letter and passport will be checked. You will pass through security screening. Some items — including certain electronics — may need to be left outside or checked in.
tutorial.visual:
Entry sequence
Appointment letter check at gate
Security screening (bag + personal)
Document receipt / number assignment
Wait in designated area

tutorial.label: Step 4 of 8
tutorial.heading: Biometrics — fingerprints and photo
tutorial.instruction: Before your consular interview, you will be called to provide biometrics — fingerprints and a digital photograph. This is routine and applies to almost all immigrant visa applicants.
tutorial.visual:
Biometric collection
Fingerprints are scanned digitally. You will also be photographed. This takes only a few minutes. Follow the staff instructions exactly.

tutorial.label: Step 5 of 8
tutorial.heading: The consular interview window
tutorial.instruction: You will be called to a consular window. The officer will review your documents, ask questions about your relationship, background, and immigration history. Answer concisely and truthfully. Do not volunteer information beyond what is asked.
tutorial.note: Consistency is critical. Your answers must align with your DS-260 responses and the documents you submitted during NVC processing.
tutorial.visual:
Common interview questions
How did you meet your spouse?
When and where was your marriage?
What does your petitioner do for work?
Have you visited the United States before?
Where will you live in the United States?

tutorial.label: Step 6 of 8
tutorial.heading: Document review at the window
tutorial.instruction: The officer may ask you to produce specific original documents. Present them calmly and in the order requested. Having a well-organized packet makes this faster and smoother.
tutorial.visual:
Be ready to produce
Original passport(s)
Marriage certificate / Nikah Nama
Birth certificate
Police clearance certificate
Affidavit of Support
Passport photos

tutorial.label: Step 7 of 8
tutorial.heading: Stay calm — the officer is doing their job
tutorial.instruction: Consular officers ask direct questions. Their tone is professional, not personal. Nervousness is expected and normal. Answer clearly and calmly. If you do not understand a question, politely ask for clarification.
tutorial.visual: Answer only what is asked. Be honest. Be calm. Be concise. You have prepared for this — trust your preparation.

tutorial.label: Step 8 of 8
tutorial.heading: Possible outcomes after the interview
tutorial.instruction: The officer will indicate the outcome at the window or shortly after. The three main outcomes are approval, Administrative Processing (AP), or refusal. If AP applies, proceed to Step 9 to track and manage the AP process.
tutorial.visual:
What you may hear
Approved — passport retained, visa to be delivered Best
Administrative Processing — more time needed Step 9
Refused — written reason provided Consult attorney

explainer.title: AP is not a refusal — it means more review is needed
explainer.body: Administrative Processing (AP) occurs when the consulate needs additional time to review your case background, security checks, or has requested additional documents. Most AP cases resolve and result in visa issuance. Timelines vary significantly and are outside Rahvana's or the applicant's control.

recorder.title: Record your AP details
recorder.subtitle: Save this now so Rahvana can track and remind you

info_sections.title: What to do during Administrative Processing
items: Check CEAC status regularly — aim for weekly checks without obsessing over it daily
If additional documents were requested, submit them promptly and exactly as specified
Monitor the email address you registered with the consulate for any correspondence
Log each CEAC status check in the update log above to track any changes over time
Ensure your passport remains valid — if AP extends significantly, verify validity
If AP extends beyond 180 days, consider consulting an immigration attorney about options

info_sections.title: What Administrative Processing does not mean
items: AP is not a visa refusal — your case is still being reviewed
AP does not mean there is a problem with your relationship or documents
Most AP cases eventually result in visa issuance — though no timeline can be guaranteed
Contacting the embassy frequently typically does not speed up the process and may not receive a useful response
